10.text: A different change passes its checks, but Git refuses permission to create the commit. The files are edited. Is the review finished, still unfinished with its edits saved, or should the server commit for Codex?

11.text: Step four. A transcript is the saved conversation. Match active Codex identity and repo, not the newest session. If this file is unreadable, Codex first tries its supported read-only conversation export. If that fails, it asks you for a readable copy or path for this specific conversation and checks that it belongs to this session and project. If none is readable, stop and name the missing conversation. Record the conversation’s path, fingerprint and size in the explainer’s source list. The private text stays outside Git.

12.text: The connected session closes, then a question arrives. Yesterday’s headless setting exists. Does the question launch work, vanish, or stay saved?

13.text: Step five tests the same player in the ordinary browser and beside Codex in a terminal workspace. Watch with sound, answer choices, leave comments, and press Send. Codex receives the saved review; you see which scenes changed after revision. Check the printed address opens this plan, even when another server occupies the first port. Then test a separate portable copy elsewhere: only that disconnected copy needs a file returned to the agent. Your chosen scope A stays the same.

15.text: Step six needs all five steps. A real scratch project installs, builds a narrated plan, reviews and revises, implements, passes independent code check, shows a walkthrough, fixes a flagged choice and commits. Exercise questions, headless changes, failure recovery and session discovery. Record commands, versions, durations and results. Fast and full touched specs plus Claude regressions protect existing behavior. Untested live paths and platforms remain unverified.

17.text: Mocked queue specs pass, but no real Codex session has answered a page question. Can the complete lifecycle be called tested?

18.text: The revised plan keeps your chosen local scope. Send here needs no download. One shared workflow and small agent adapters keep the code easy to extend. Failed commits remain unfinished. The guide holds the full examples and interfaces. Approve this clearer plan or ask for changes; implementation follows approval.

01.text: You should be able to finish the same review loop with Codex or Claude Code. This proposal changes installation, review follow-up, conversation discovery and lifecycle proof. The branch is feat/codex-first-class; integration behavior remains proposed.

02.text: The goal is the same review experience with either agent: watch with sound, answer choices, leave comments, press Send and see the revised video. Codex plugins install instructions. Trusted hooks trigger commands; tool connections expose services. These are extension options, not a complete hosted review system. The existing browser player handles review. We will test a browser beside Codex in the terminal. A hosted Claude page also saves reviews, checks reviewer identity and answers questions. We have not found a proven Codex replacement for those services.

03.text: You chose A: finish the local Codex workflow and check portable reviews. That scope is settled. Local Send goes directly to the project and notifies Codex. Automatic delivery from a hosted page elsewhere stays outside this change.

04.text: On this machine, press Send. The project saves your answers and comments, then the waiting Codex session receives the review. That is how your first review reached us: you did not download anything. A file transfer is needed only for a disconnected portable copy reviewed elsewhere.

05.text: Good code means one shared review workflow: save, notify, review and fix, then commit. Small agent adapters contain only the differences: check available features, launch with the right permissions, notify the right session, and find its saved conversation. Each function receives this project and the relevant review or session, then reports what happened. Shared code owns retries and decides when work is finished. Adding another agent should mean adding those small functions. Keep one player, one server and one inbox, the saved pending reviews. Earlier answers still bind the plan; independent checks and real walkthroughs still apply. The guide holds the exact function contract.

07.text: Step two uses the feature checks from step one. Starting Codex with no session open is enabled only when you ask. It must follow the allowed permissions and preserve commit signing. Here is the failure case: the files were edited, but the signing key is unavailable. The commit fails. The work is still unfinished. The review page shows Stopped before commit and the log. Keep the edits. You restore the signing key or settings; Codex then uses the guarded retry command, checking for any live worker and any work already finished. Only a successful commit allows the review to be marked done.

08.text: A teammate installs the plugin without video tools. Does installation prove the lifecycle, or should diagnostics name missing tools?

09.text: Step three uses installation and the safe follow-up from step two. First save the review. Then notify the session already waiting, or the verified connected Codex session. If neither is available, use an explicitly configured new run; otherwise keep the review for the next session. Only one agent handles the saved item. Notification means the message arrived, not that the work finished. Ask about this saves a question for a live session. Its reply appears on this page. A disconnected question waits rather than starting a new run.
